title: Normalize Struggle
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: The tenth and final Will to Learn strategy, Normalize Struggle exists to interrupt the hamster wheel effect in which students interpret difficulty as proof they uniquely don't belong. Stuart lays out a three-step method: making difficulty normal via whole-class polling and student-as-expert testimonials, making critical feedback normal via Geoffrey Cohen's magic feedback line, and making difficulty desirable via a classroom do hard things ethos and a colleague's Motivation Mondays using short Jocko Willink videos. The guide closes with an extended personal narrative about a student named Lindsay, showing how a single honest MGC conversation redirected months of quiet self-comparison and anti-Belonging.
points: Stuart's whole-class polling technique reliably shows the majority of students share the same anxiety, letting him reframe struggle as normal rather than personal.

Geoffrey Cohen's magic feedback line was shown in research to make students more likely to revise essays and trust teachers, simply by pairing critical feedback with an explicit statement of high expectations.

A colleague's Motivation Mondays, built on short Jocko Willink video clips, works because it requires minimal prep, uses a novel and credible outside voice, and drops in occasionally rather than eating large blocks of class time.

The Lindsay story shows normalize-struggle work as slow gardening, not button-pushing, since real change came only after Stuart got specific in a one-on-one MGC conversation about self-comparison to peers.
quotes: This creates a hamster-wheel effect in their mind, making them hyper-alert to any other signals from your classroom that they don't fit.
Every single time that I've done this after a whole-class speaking event like a Pop-Up Debate, upwards of 70 percent of my students have raised their hands.
Those who received the magical line were more likely to make revisions to their essays and indicate that they trusted their teachers.
What we want here is to make it odd and unseemly to not seek some measure of challenge in a given class.
Five Key Beliefs work is gardening, not button-pushing. You control only so much. Sometimes the pains you seek to mend are stubbornly resilient.
What if the whole goal this semester was for Lindsay in three months to be someone stronger and smarter and more capable than Lindsay today?
